newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus removes last nuclear missiles to Russia.
newsitem.headline: Belarus removes last nuclear missiles to Russia.

text.p: Belarus has given a boost to world nuclear disarmament by sending the last of its Soviet-era nuclear warheads for destruction, officials in the capital of the former Soviet republic said on Friday.
"The missiles have all gone," presidential aide Vladimir Zametalin told Reuters.

President Alexander Lukashenko, who signed a Russia-mediated deal with his parliamentary foes overnight, had threatened to keep the last 18 of 72 SS-25 strategic missiles as a bargaining chip against NATO's plans to expand eastwards.

Zametalin said the truck-based rockets had been removed in the last few days. But other sources who asked not to be named said the last of them went on Thursday in line with the START-1 international arms reduction treaty.
Belarus, a republic of 10 million bordering Russia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Ukraine, was the only former Soviet state outside Russia which still had missiles on its soil.

The deadline for removing them was fixed as the end of 1996 under the so-called "Lisbon protocol" of 1992 settling with the United States the fate of missiles left outside Russia when the Soviet Union broke up.
Ukraine and Kazakhstan had sent their warheads for destruction in Russia well ahead of the deadline.
All the missiles in Belarus remained under Russian control after the Soviet Union fell apart in 1991 and they could not be launched without Moscow's command.

But Lukashenko, an outspoken opponent of NATO and its plans to let central and eastern European countries join the Western alliance, hinted he might keep the last of the missiles when he addressed the Russian parliament earlier this month.

"Withdrawal (of the missiles) from Belarus could be interrupted if NATO does not offer guarantees that nuclear arms will not be deployed in eastern European states which are candidates for membership in the alliance," he said.
However Russian officials immediately squashed the idea.

News of the missiles' departure came hours after Lukashenko and his parliamentary opponents reached a compromise, mediated by Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, in a row over the president's wish to extend his powers.

"We (Belarus) promised to ship all the nuclear missiles to Russia by the end of the year and we have fulfilled our promises," one Belarussian source said. "The last strategic missile was transferred yesterday."
Belarus was home to modern, truck-based missiles with a single warhead each.
Minsk ratified both the START-1 and nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty in February 1993.
Some Russian politicians were also keen to keep Belarussian missiles, like Alexander Shokhin, parliament's deputy speaker.

"This issue should be linked to NATO expansion or to the answer to our permanent question -- does NATO plan to deploy nuclear arms on the territories of its new members?" Russia's Itar-Tass news agency quoted him as saying recently.
NATO says it has no plans to deploy nuclear weapons on the territory of new member states but is reluctant to promise formally never to do so.
